job: Fresh graduate in computing and engineering
name: Grace Okafor

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking with me. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me both what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a junior developer at a logistics software firm in Manchester, working on the screen that tells warehouse staff where to put pallets. Mornings are stand-up, then fixing small bugs, and in the afternoon my team lead, Priya, reviews what I wrote. I rent a room in a flat near Piccadilly, and my mum, who's a nurse in Salford, can't send money because she's helping my sister with school.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like most and least about it?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the moment a bug I fixed makes a warehouse worker's job easier. I don't like checking my bank balance on payday, because after rent and the loan payment there's about 60 left. I've got maybe three weeks of cushion, and I count it often.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's look at AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's what I expected, a useful assistant and not much more. I use the code helper now and then for boring bits, and I'd tell my friends that it saves me twenty minutes a day, not twenty hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, my job is okay in that world, but okay isn't the same as safe. The firm is small, and if it loses one big client, juniors go first. My pay barely covers the loan, so even slow times feel risky.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working and use the helper a little more to get through tickets faster, so Priya notices me. I'd put 100 a month into a savings pot to build one month of cover, which means no more takeaway on Fridays. I'd also start a small side project, an app for hospital rotas, since my mum would use it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine, honestly. A bit tense about money, but not about the future, because the way things are now is manageable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said juniors go first if a client leaves. Has that crossed your mind lately?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, in March a client left and two contractors were let go within a month. I'm on a permanent contract, but I know a permanent contract only means longer notice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why a hospital rota app in particular?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My mum swaps shifts on a group chat with twenty nurses, and it takes her an hour every week. If I built something simple, it'd help her and maybe sell to other wards.

say: It's a **useful assistant**, saving twenty minutes a day, not twenty hours.
I'd keep telling friends there's no need to panic.
think: The firm is small, so one lost client would hit **juniors** first.
My pay barely covers the loan, so even slow times feel **risky**.
do: Put **100 a month** into savings and drop Friday takeaway.
Use the code helper more to clear tickets faster and get noticed.
Start a **hospital rota** app on weekends as a side project.
feel: **Fine** overall, with some tension about money rather than the future.
S0.quote: I'd tell my friends that it saves me twenty minutes a day, not twenty hours.
fieldNote: Her unease is about a **small firm** and thin money, not about AI.
Open and practical; side project is rooted in her mother's real problem.
Permanent contract gives some comfort but she knows its limit.

steps.text: Move 100 a month into a savings pot
Use the code helper on routine tickets to finish faster
Build a simple hospital shift-swap app on weekends
Stop Friday takeaway meals

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's look at Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's real and we should get ready. Writing code is one of the things the card names, so I'd tell my team lead we should learn the new tools together instead of waiting to be told.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm worried that junior coding is the first thing to shrink. The firm needs fewer people to write the simple code I write now. I'm not sure I'd have a job in three years unless I move up fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take every course the firm pays for and use the AI tools daily, so I can review their code and not only write my own. I'd ask Priya to put me on the design side of the next project. I'd also keep three months of rent saved as soon as I can, even if it takes two years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious but also interested. It's like being told the road ahead has changed, and you have to learn to read new signs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you mean by reviewing their code?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If a tool writes a hundred lines, someone has to check it's right and safe. That someone needs judgement, and I think I can build judgement faster than a lot of people if I sit with seniors.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you cut if work got slower?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The gym membership first, 28 a month, then phone data. Rent I can't cut unless I find a cheaper room, and I'd ask my flatmate about that in the first month.

say: It's real, and I'd tell my team lead we should **learn the tools** together.
I'd say juniors need proper training, not just lower expectations.
think: Simple code is the first thing to shrink, and **junior coders** are the ones doing it.
Unless I move up fast, I might not have this job in **three years**.
do: Take every **paid course** and use AI tools daily to review their code.
Ask Priya for a place on the **design side** of the next project.
Build **three months** of rent as savings over two years.
feel: **Anxious but interested**, like learning to read new road signs.
S1.quote: If a tool writes a hundred lines, someone has to check it's right and safe. That someone needs judgement
fieldNote: She turns worry into a **learning plan** quickly.
Aims to become the person who reviews machine code rather than writes it.
Her mood is anxious because junior coding is directly exposed.

steps.text: Take every course the firm pays for this year
Use AI coding tools daily and review the output line by line
Save three months of rent over two years
Cancel the gym membership and cut phone data

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's look at AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say two years is not enough time for anyone, and I'd be honest about being scared. I'd tell friends to talk to their MPs and ask what the plan is for people who just started paying a loan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I think my job goes in 2028. Junior software work is the first thing a thinking AI does well, and the robots coming in 2031 are no help to me. I'd be out of work with a loan and no one to lean on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop everything that isn't rent, food and the loan. I'd look for any work that's hands-on or local, like warehouse systems support or a hospital IT team, where people still need people nearby. I'd move into a cheaper room and ask my mum whether I could stay in Salford for a couple of months if I lost the job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. My stomach drops, and I keep thinking of the date on the card as a deadline for me, personally.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said hospital IT might still need people nearby. What makes you think so?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hospitals are slow to change and full of old systems, and the ward managers I've met like a person they can ring. It's a guess, but it's a better guess than the startup world.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your sister?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her to keep studying and not to panic, and I'd tell her I'll still send her what I can. I just wouldn't tell her how little that might be.

say: Two years is **not enough time**, and I'd ask MPs what the plan is.
I'd admit I'm scared instead of pretending to be fine.
think: Junior software work is what a thinking AI does well first, so **my job goes**.
The robots in 2031 don't help me in the **gap between**.
do: Cut everything except **rent, food** and the loan.
Look for **hospital IT** or local support roles where people still want a person.
Ask my mum if I could stay in **Salford** briefly.
feel: **Alarmed**, with a drop in my stomach whenever I see the date.
S2.quote: Hospitals are slow to change and full of old systems, and the ward managers I've met like a person they can ring.
fieldNote: She expects to lose her job and says so plainly.
Her plan shifts toward **local, human-facing** work that changes slowly.
Worries about being unable to help her sister.

steps.text: Cancel everything except rent, food and loan payments
Apply for hospital IT and local support roles
Move to a cheaper room within a month
Ask my mum if I can stay in Salford if needed

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's look at AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is enough to pivot, but not to relax. I'd tell people at work to start now, because a couple of years in this line is a good start in the wrong direction if the field is closing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'd have three good working years. After that, I'd want to be in something where a human stays in the loop, like safety checks, healthcare systems or teaching others to use the tools. I'd also want the loan cleared before the change hits.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay in the job for two years and pay the loan hard, then take a part-time master's in health informatics. I'd go for hospital data work, which pays less at first but is steadier. I'd keep applying to learn AI tools so I can sell myself as someone who works with them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: More hopeful than with two years. Five years gives me a plan, and a plan is what I need.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why a master's, rather than staying in the job and learning on the side?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A master's in health informatics gets me a recognised name and a route into hospitals. On my own I'd learn, but nobody would hire me on the strength of my evenings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you pay for it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the firm to part-fund it and pay the rest by working weekends on the rota app. I don't have a back-up. If it doesn't work, I'd delay, not borrow more.

say: Five years is enough to **pivot**, but not to relax.
I'd tell colleagues to start learning now, not later.
think: I'd have about **three good years** in this field, and then I need a human-in-the-loop role.
I want the loan **cleared** before the shift hits.
do: Stay two years, pay the loan hard, then study **health informatics** part-time.
Ask the firm to **part-fund** the master's.
Keep using AI tools so I can sell myself as someone who works with them.
feel: **More hopeful**, because five years gives me a plan.
S3.quote: A master's in health informatics gets me a recognised name and a route into hospitals.
fieldNote: She picks health informatics because it ties to her mother's world.
Still anxious because the plan needs money she doesn't have.

steps.text: Apply for a part-time master's in health informatics
Pay 300 a month toward the loan for two years
Keep using AI tools daily to show I can work with them
Ask the firm to part-fund the master's

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's look at AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years is long enough to get ready. I'd say it's a good moment to learn something solid and not panic, and I'd tell friends that the people who plan early will do fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think ten years is a real gift. I'd be 32, and by then I could be in a senior role or somewhere that people still choose a person. Even so, I'd want a plan B in case things move faster than the card says.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the job, clear the loan in five years, and build the hospital rota app into a real product. I'd keep learning the tools every year, since they'll keep changing. I might also save for a deposit, which sounds odd with AGI coming, but I'd still want somewhere to live.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm for the most part. A little guilty, too, because I know others have less time to prepare than I do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why would you save for a deposit if you expect AGI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because a home is still a home. If things go badly I'd have somewhere to live, and if they go well I'd still have it. It's the one plan that works either way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about the guilt you mentioned?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My mum's friends in nursing have no plan B, and neither do the warehouse workers on my screens. I'd want my side project to help them, not just me.

say: Ten years is long enough, and **early planners** will do fine.
I'd tell friends to learn something solid and skip the panic.
think: Ten years is a **real gift**, and I'd still want a plan B.
I'd expect to be in a senior role, or in work where people prefer a **person**.
do: Clear the loan in **five years** and then save for a deposit.
Grow the rota app into a **real product** for hospitals.
Keep learning the new tools every year.
feel: **Calm** mostly, with some guilt about people with less time.
S4.quote: A home is still a home. If things go badly I'd have somewhere to live, and if they go well I'd still have it.
fieldNote: Time lowers her mood to **uneasy**; she is still tight on money.
Moral concern for people with less preparation, such as nurses and warehouse staff.
Wants a plan that works whichever way things go.

steps.text: Clear the student loan within five years
Grow the rota app into a product for hospital wards
Learn one new AI tool every year
Save for a house deposit once the loan is paid

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. I'd have no time and little money, and my mum couldn't help. What would help is a loan system that pauses payments if you lose work, and training that's free and aimed at jobs that exist.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Just that people my age are not clueless about this. A lot of us are already trying things, and what we need is fair rules and some patience.

headlineQuote: A lot of us are already trying things, and what we need is fair rules and some patience.
portrait: Grace, 22, is a top-of-the-class software engineering graduate, now a junior developer at a **logistics software firm** in Manchester.
She rents a room, carries heavy debt and has about three weeks of money saved, with no family help.
She is progressive and steady, uses AI tools now and then, and turns worry into a learning plan.
She expects junior coding to shrink first and steers toward **hospital systems**, where her mother works.
Her mood runs from uneasy to alarmed, depending on how much time she has to get ready.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** scenario worries her most, because she would lose the job with no time or cushion.
whatWouldHelp: A loan system that **pauses payments** if work ends, plus free training aimed at jobs that really exist.
